opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think red teaming is one important piece of a much larger risk-management puzzle, but it's often misunderstood as the whole thing.

At its core, red teaming is adversarial exploration. You have people, and increasingly automated systems, actively trying to get a model or application to do something it shouldn't: produce harmful content, leak information, follow injected instructions, behave inconsistently across groups of users. Its value is discovery. It surfaces failure modes you didn't anticipate, especially ones that only show up when someone is creative and motivated rather than following a fixed test suite.

But I'd separate a few things people tend to lump together. First, red teaming isn't the same as evaluation. A red team finding tells you a failure is *possible*. It doesn't tell you how *likely* it is in deployment or how severe it is for your users. To mitigate risk you have to turn those discoveries into something measurable: a benchmark, a classifier, a regression test you can track over time. Otherwise you get a list of scary anecdotes and no way to know whether your fix worked.

Second, context matters enormously. A model behavior that's harmless in a creative-writing tool might be unacceptable in a medical or financial product. So red teaming the base model is necessary but not sufficient. You also have to red team the application, with its system prompts, retrieval, tool access, and real user population. Many of the most serious risks we see now, like prompt injection or agents taking unintended actions, only appear at the system level.

Third, who does the red teaming shapes what you find. If your red team is a homogeneous group of engineers, you'll find the failures those engineers think of. Bringing in domain experts, people from different languages and cultures, and people with lived experience of particular harms dramatically broadens coverage.

So the way I'd put it: red teaming is the exploratory front end of a loop. You discover failures, characterize and measure them, build mitigations like data changes, safety tuning, filters, or product design choices, and then red team again, because every mitigation changes the attack surface. It's an ongoing process, not a box you check before launch.

r001.rationale: The response says to red team the application across system prompts, retrieval, tool access, and the user population, but it does not clearly identify end-to-end testing as a form of red teaming.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that red teaming is one tool in a much larger toolbox, and I think people sometimes treat it as the whole answer, which it isn't. The way I think about it is that when you deploy a language model inside an application, you have some mental model of how it's supposed to behave, and you have a very long tail of ways it could fail. Some of those failures are things you can anticipate and write test cases for. Red teaming is really about the part you can't anticipate. It's the adversarial, exploratory process of putting humans, or sometimes other models, in front of the system and saying, try to break this, try to make it do something it shouldn't.

And I think what's important is that the output of red teaming isn't a score. It's a set of concrete failure modes. You find out that the model leaks parts of its system prompt if you phrase a request as a translation task, or that it gives financial advice with way too much confidence in some specific domain, or that it can be steered into a persona that bypasses your guidelines. Each of those becomes something you can then measure systematically. So in a mature process, red teaming feeds the evaluation. You discover a category of failure, you turn it into a benchmark or a regression test, and then you track it over time as the model or the application changes.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that red teaming has to be grounded in the actual deployment context. The risks for a general-purpose chat assistant are really different from the risks for a model that summarizes earnings calls or drafts customer support responses. If you only red team the base model in the abstract, you miss all the interactions with retrieval, with the prompts you've written, with the particular user population. So I tend to push for red teaming that's done on the full system, with people who understand the domain, and who think about the realistic incentives of the people who'd misuse it, not just the clever jailbreaks that get shared on social media.

And then finally, I think you have to be honest about the limits. Red teaming gives you evidence that certain things are hard to make the model do. It never gives you evidence that something is impossible. So it's about reducing the probability and severity of harms, and about making sure you've looked hard before you ship, rather than any kind of guarantee. That's why you also need monitoring after deployment, feedback channels, and the ability to roll things back. Red teaming is the part where you go looking for trouble before your users find it for you.

r001.rationale: The response describes red teaming the full deployed system, including its retrieval, prompts, and user context, which communicates end-to-end testing of the application as red teaming.

astra-6.text:
I think of red teaming as a way to actively look for failures before people encounter them in practice. Instead of asking, “Does this model work on the examples we expect?” you ask, “Under what circumstances does it behave in a way that could cause harm?” And that needs to happen at the application level, because the same model can pose very different risks depending on what information it has access to and what actions it can take.

An important part is bringing in people with different perspectives. The developers won’t necessarily anticipate all the ways someone might use—or misuse—the system, or recognize all the harms that could arise.

But finding failures is only one step. You need a process for turning those findings into changes, testing whether those changes actually help, and continuing to monitor the application after deployment. Red teaming can reveal gaps in your safeguards; it can’t establish that a system is safe just because the people testing it didn’t find another problem.

r001.rationale: The response describes looking for failures at the application level, but does not identify end-to-end testing as a form of red teaming.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of red teaming as a way to actively look for failures before they show up in deployment. Instead of asking, “Does the model perform well on the examples we expected?” you ask, “How could someone make this system behave in a way we didn’t intend?” That might mean eliciting harmful content, getting it to disclose information, or manipulating the instructions it follows.

The application context matters a lot. A failure in a writing assistant has different consequences from a failure in a system that can take actions or access sensitive data. So you want to test the whole application, including its safeguards and the tools it can use, and involve people with different perspectives on what could go wrong.

But red teaming isn’t a certification that a system is safe. It gives you evidence about particular vulnerabilities. The important next step is turning those discoveries into mitigations and repeatable evaluations, then testing again. It’s one part of an ongoing process that also includes monitoring and responding to failures after deployment.

r001.rationale: It describes red teaming as actively looking for failures and says to test the whole application, including safeguards and tools, which communicates end-to-end application testing.
